front: Question shape: concept T/F. How do you attack it?
back: Read every word; one wrong qualifier ("always", "both", "in Java and OCaml") makes it false. Typical targets: == vs =, null vs None, array length, records of closures as objects.

front: Question shape: "Is this tail recursive?" What do you check?
back: Find every recursive call. TR only if each one is the whole result of its branch (nothing left to do after it returns). Then, if asked, rewrite with an accumulator helper.

front: Question shape: trace a mystery function on a queue/deque picture.
back: Copy the starting picture, then step the loop one node at a time, redrawing every pointer write (next, prev, head, tail) in order. Mark new nodes. Finish by checking head, tail and the last node's next.

front: Question shape: which invariant is broken (1, 2a, 2b, ... 2f)?
back: Check (1) first: both None or both Some. Then each numbered clause separately against the picture. Name exactly the clauses that fail; a picture can break several.

front: Question shape: code → heap, or heap → code ("which programs build this picture?").
back: Every literal/constructor/record expression allocates a new heap cell; a variable reuses the cell it names. Count heap cells and arrows; extra stack bindings also make a picture differ.

front: Question shape: == vs = on a picture.
back: == is true only if both sides are the same arrow target (same heap cell). = walks the structure. Remember expressions like Some a allocate a fresh cell, so c.y == Some a is false even when c.y = Some a is true.

front: Question shape: closures in the ASM (bindings at HERE, what the closure saves, type, what prints).
back: Stack bindings at a point = top-level lets so far plus locals in scope. A closure saves the free identifiers its body uses (not its own parameters). Each call of a maker creates fresh state.

front: Question shape: queue/deque programming. Checklist before you hand it in?
back: Empty case; one-element case; head AND tail updated; tail's next = None (deque: head's prev = None); both None when emptied; tail recursive if asked; generic types ('a queue); only the allowed library functions.

front: Question shape: write a (property-based) test.
back: Record to_list before; run the operation; compare to_list after with the pure-list answer (e.g. l1 @ l2); also check valid q and any emptied structure. Return a bool combining them with &&.

front: Question shape: GUI build (fill in the blanks).
back: Recipe: state (ref or make_controller) → repaint reads the state → canvas size repaint gives (widget, notifier_controller) → add_event_listener with a listener that updates state → return the widget (and controller if the type says so).

front: Question shape: GUI edit analysis (compiles? same appearance? same function?).
back: Answer the three separately. Type errors → won't compile. Changing draw order, borders, layout → appearance. Removing/moving listeners or not returning a controller → function. An edit can keep appearance but change function.

front: Question shape: Java "what happens?"
back: Pick one: compile error, runtime exception, or output. Check static vs instance, types, null (NullPointerException), bounds (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException), == vs .equals.

front: Question shape: Java 2D-array method.
back: Write the loop bounds first (r < a.length, c < a[r].length for ragged). Handle null/edge cases the spec names. Allocate with new int[m][n]. Use a helper for neighbour/sub-array checks.

front: Question shape: "explain in English".
back: One or two precise sentences naming the mechanism (which pointer, which invariant, which listener). Don't restate the code.

front: Is int option the same type as int? What does that buy you?
back: No. 'a option is a different type, so the compiler forces you to handle None before using the value (unlike Java null).

front: Some x == Some x: true or false? How should you compare options?
back: False in the ASM model: each Some allocates a new cell. Compare options by pattern matching (or = for structure), never ==.

front: What's the difference between None and Some [] for an 'a list option?
back: None means "no answer / absent"; Some [] means "the answer is the empty list". Partial functions return None when they have no result.

front: How do you write a partial function like last : 'a list -> 'a option?
back: Match: [] -> None | [x] -> Some x | _ :: tl -> last tl. Return None instead of failwith for the missing case.

front: In e1; e2, what type should e1 have, and what does the whole expression return?
back: e1 should have type unit (otherwise a warning); the expression evaluates e1 for its effect, then returns e2's value.

front: Where may ;; appear, and is a trailing ; allowed?
back: ;; is only for top-level phrases (e.g. ;; run_test ...). Don't put ; after the last expression of a sequence: e1; e2; then end/in is a syntax trap.

front: What is fun () -> ... used for?
back: A thunk: delays work until called with (). Used for listeners/actions (e.g. mouseclick_listener f calls f ()).

front: What is the only value of type unit, and what type do field writes and print_int have?
back: (). r.f <- v, print_int, and List.iter all return unit.

front: What does {r with g = v} do to r?
back: Nothing: it allocates a NEW record copying r's other fields with g = v. So {r with g = v} == r is false.

front: How do you declare and update a mutable field? What does the update return?
back: type t = {mutable f : int}. r.f <- 3 updates in place and has type unit. Only fields declared mutable can be assigned.

front: A function mutates a record field of its parameter. Does the caller see the change?
back: Yes. The parameter is a reference to the same heap record, so the caller's record changes too.

front: let b = a where a is a mutable record. What's on the heap?
back: One record; a and b both point to it (aliases). b.f <- 1 is visible through a.

front: Do two identical literals {f = 1} and {f = 1} share a heap cell?
back: No. Every record/constructor expression allocates a fresh cell; only binding an existing value (let b = a) shares.

front: What is 'a ref, and what are ref e, !e and e := v sugar for?
back: type 'a ref = {mutable contents : 'a}. ref e = {contents = e}; !e = e.contents; e := v is e.contents <- v.

front: How can you test whether two records are aliases?
back: == (physical equality): true iff they are the same heap cell. Or mutate one and see if the other changes.

front: What are the three parts of the OCaml ASM, and what lives in each?
back: Workspace: the expression being simplified. Stack: bindings (identifier → value or arrow), plus saved workspaces during calls. Heap: records, constructor cells (Cons, Some), closures.

front: ASM rule for let x = v in e (v a value)?
back: Push the binding x → v on the stack, continue with e. (Top-level lets stay on the stack.)

front: ASM rule for a constructor or record expression whose parts are values?
back: Allocate a new heap cell holding the fields; the workspace gets an arrow (reference) to it.

front: ASM rule for an identifier in the workspace?
back: Look up the most recent binding on the stack and replace the identifier with its value (copying the arrow, not the heap cell).

front: ASM rule for fun x -> e?
back: Allocate a closure on the heap: the function code plus the saved bindings of the free identifiers it uses. The workspace gets an arrow to it.

front: ASM rule for a function call (f v)?
back: Save the current workspace with a hole where the call was; push the closure's saved bindings and the parameter bindings; the body becomes the workspace.

front: ASM rule for returning from a call?
back: When the body is a value: pop the call's bindings off the stack, restore the saved workspace and plug the value into the hole.

front: ASM rules for r.f and r.f <- v?
back: Read: follow the arrow and copy the field's value. Write: follow the arrow and overwrite the field in the heap cell; result is ().

front: ASM rules for if and match?
back: if true/false picks a branch. match: compare the value against patterns in order; pattern variables are pushed as stack bindings for the chosen branch.

front: What does = (structural equality) do, and when does it fail?
back: Walks both structures comparing contents. Loops forever on cyclic data; raises an exception when it reaches functions.

front: What does == check? Which equates more things, = or ==?
back: == checks same heap location (same arrow target). == equates strictly fewer things: a == b implies a = b, not the reverse.

front: Java's == on objects vs .equals?
back: == is reference equality (same object). .equals is whatever the class defines (String compares characters). Arrays don't override equals, so it's reference equality.

front: Write the HW4 queue types.
back:
type 'a qnode = { v : 'a; mutable next : 'a qnode option }
type 'a queue = { mutable head : 'a qnode option; mutable tail : 'a qnode option }

front: State the queue invariant.
back: (1) head and tail are both None, or (2) head = Some n1 and tail = Some n2 where (2a) n2 is reachable from n1 by following next, and (2b) n2.next = None.

front: Implement enq.
back:
let enq (x : 'a) (q : 'a queue) : unit =
  let n = Some { v = x; next = None } in
  begin match q.tail with
  | None -> q.head <- n; q.tail <- n
  | Some t -> t.next <- n; q.tail <- n
  end

front: Implement deq (fail on empty).
What breaks if deq leaves out if n.next = None then q.tail <- None?
back: Dequeuing the last element leaves head = None but tail = Some n: violates invariant (1)/(2), and the next enq links onto a dead node so the queue loses elements.

front: Pattern for iterating over a queue (e.g. length) tail-recursively?
back:
let rec loop (no : 'a qnode option) (acc : int) : int =
  begin match no with
  | None -> acc
  | Some n -> loop n.next (acc + 1)
  end
in loop q.head 0

front: What's wrong with a queue whose single node's next points to itself (head = tail = that node)?
back: (2a) still holds but (2b) fails: tail.next = Some node, not None. Iterating with next would loop forever.

front: When is a recursive call a tail call?
back: When it is the whole result: nothing remains to do after it returns. E.g. the entire branch of an if/match, the right operand of && or ||, or the last expression in a sequence.

front: Name positions where a recursive call is NOT a tail call.
back: As an argument (f (g x), not (loop tl)), under an operator (1 + loop tl, x :: loop tl), the left operand of && / ||, inside an if condition, or followed by ; more code.

front: hd && mystery tl vs mystery tl && hd: which is tail recursive?
back: hd && mystery tl is tail recursive (right operand; && short-circuits). mystery tl && hd is not (the result is still tested afterwards).

front: How do you rewrite a list function tail-recursively?
back: Add a helper with an accumulator: loop rest acc. Base case returns acc (reverse it once if you built a list with ::).

front: Why avoid acc @ [x] in a loop?
back: @ copies its left list each time: quadratic. Cons onto the accumulator (x :: acc) and reverse once at the end.

front: Why do queue/deque functions need to be tail recursive?
back: A tail call reuses the stack frame, so long queues don't overflow the stack. The large-input tests (and exam rubrics) check this.

front: "Must be tail recursive and exit early": what does each half require?
back: TR: every recursive call in tail position. Exit early: stop as soon as the answer is known (e.g. (seen <= count) && loop ...) instead of always walking the whole queue.

front: Write the HW4 deque types.
back:
type 'a dqnode = { v : 'a; mutable next : 'a dqnode option; mutable prev : 'a dqnode option }
type 'a deque = { mutable head : 'a dqnode option; mutable tail : 'a dqnode option }

front: State the deque invariant (1, 2a–2f).
back: (1) head and tail both None, or (2) head = Some n1, tail = Some n2 and: (2a) n2 reachable from n1 via next; (2b) n2.next = None; (2c) n1 reachable from n2 via prev; (2d) n1.prev = None; (2e) for every node n, n.next = Some m implies m.prev = Some n; (2f) n.prev = Some m implies m.next = Some n.

front: The deque mirror rule?
back: Every change to a next pointer needs the matching prev change (and vice versa), or (2e)/(2f) break.

front: remove_head: what are the two non-empty cases?
back: One element (head == tail): set head and tail to None. Several: head <- n.next, and the new head's prev <- None. Return n.v.

front: Reversing a deque in place: what must you save before swapping a node's pointers?
back: The old next (let nx = n.next) before n.next <- n.prev; n.prev <- nx; then continue from nx. Finally swap head and tail.

front: Appending deque d2 onto d1 when both are non-empty: which four pointers change?
back: d1's tail node .next <- d2.head; d2's head node .prev <- d1.tail; d1.tail <- d2.tail; then empty d2 (head and tail None).

front: Recipe for a property-based test of a mutating deque/queue function.
back: let before = to_list q in op q; to_list q = (pure list computation on before) && valid q. Check any other structure it should empty, too.

front: Which bindings does a closure save?
back: The free identifiers its body uses: everything it refers to except its own parameters and names bound inside it. (Field names aren't identifiers.)

front: Calling a maker function (like mk_counter ()) twice: shared state or separate?
back: Separate: each call allocates a fresh ref/record, and each returned closure saves its own.

front: let g = f where f is a closure: one closure or two?
back: One. g and f are arrows to the same closure (and its saved state).

front: What is OCaml's closest analog to a Java object?
back: A record of closures that share private state (e.g. a counter record with inc and get fields closing over the same ref).

front: Write a counter maker returning a record with inc : unit -> int.
What is a widget in the course GUI library?
back: A record { repaint : Gctx.gctx -> unit; handle : Gctx.gctx -> Gctx.event -> unit; size : unit -> int * int }.

front: Does Gctx.translate change the gctx it is given?
back: No: it returns a new gctx with a shifted origin. Graphics contexts are immutable values.

front: What do border's repaint, handle and size do?
back: Draws a rectangle, then repaints the child translated by (2, 2); handle forwards events translated by (2, 2); size is the child's size + 4 in each dimension.

front: How does hpair w1 w2 route events and size itself?
back: w2 is translated by w1's width. Events go to whichever child contains the point; points in dead space (outside both) are dropped. Size: widths add, height is the max.

front: What does the event loop do with each event?
back: Calls the top widget's handle with the event, then repaints the whole top widget.

front: What does a notifier add, and in what order do its listeners run?
back: A notifier wraps a child and holds event listeners; on an event it runs the listeners (newest added first, per the course code), then passes the event to the child's handle. It doesn't change size.

front: When does mouseclick_listener f fire?
back: On MouseDown events (it calls f ()).

front: What do label, button and canvas return?
back: label s : widget * label_controller. button s : widget * label_controller * notifier_controller. canvas size repaint : widget * notifier_controller.

front: What does make_controller init give you?
back: A value_controller with get_value, change_value (sets the value and runs change listeners) and add_change_listener.

front: Recipe for a stateful widget (e.g. a clickable counter).
back: 1. state = make_controller init (or a ref). 2. repaint reads state.get_value (). 3. let w, nc = canvas size repaint. 4. nc.add_event_listener (mouseclick_listener (fun () -> state.change_value ...)). 5. return w (and state if the type asks).

front: "a" == "a" and new String("a") == "a": results?
back: true (string literals are interned, same object) and false (new always makes a new object). Use .equals for strings.

front: What is 7 / 2 in Java? And 1 + 2 + "" + 1 + 2?
back: 3 (int / int truncates). "312": + is left to right, so 1 + 2 = 3, then string concatenation.

front: What can a static method not do?
back: It has no this, so it can't use instance fields or call instance methods directly. Call it as ClassName.m().

front: Static type vs dynamic type: which decides what you may call, and which decides which code runs?
back: The static (declared) type decides which methods compile. The dynamic (runtime) class decides which implementation runs (dynamic dispatch).

front: Rules for implementing an interface?
back: Implement every method with a matching signature; interface methods are implicitly public. You can't new an interface, but you can use it as a static type.

front: Java null vs OCaml None?
back: Any Java reference type can be null; calling a method on null throws NullPointerException at runtime. OCaml's None is a separate option type, checked at compile time.

front: What does a constructor do, and what does new return?
back: new allocates an object and runs the constructor to initialise its fields (establishing invariants). new returns a reference to the object.

front: Default contents of new int[3], new boolean[3], new String[3]?
back: 0s, falses, nulls.

front: a.length: method or field? Valid indices? Can the length change?
back: A field (no parentheses). Indices 0 .. a.length - 1; anything else throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Length is fixed at allocation.

front: int[] b = a; b[0] = 9; What is a[0]?
back: 9. b and a reference the same array.

front: a.equals(b), Arrays.equals(a, b), Arrays.deepEquals(a, b) for arrays?
back: a.equals(b) is reference equality. Arrays.equals compares elements (1D). Arrays.deepEquals compares nested arrays (2D).

front: What is in new int[5][]?
back: An array of 5 rows that are all null. Allocate each row before use (a[i] = new int[k]).

front: What goes wrong with int[] row = new int[3]; for (...) grid[i] = row;?
back: Every row aliases the same array, so writing grid[0][0] changes every row. Allocate a new row per index.

front: Loop pattern for a ragged 2D array.
Which array initialisers are legal?
back: int[] a = {1, 2, 3}; and int[] a = new int[]{1, 2, 3}; are both fine. {1, 2, 3} alone only works in a declaration. new int[3]{1,2,3} is illegal.

front: Who is responsible for a class invariant?
back: The constructor establishes it and every public method preserves it. Private fields stop outside code breaking it.

front: How do you stop aliases escaping from a class that stores an array?
back: Copy the array when it comes in (constructor/setter) and when it goes out (getter). Never return the internal array itself.

front: ResArray invariant?
back: 0 <= extent <= buffer.length; if extent = 0 then every buffer entry is 0; otherwise buffer[extent - 1] is the last non-zero entry (everything from extent on is 0).

front: Java QueueImpl<E> vs the OCaml queue?
back: Same structure (QNode<E> with v and next; private head and tail), but missing links are null instead of None. Per the guide, deq on an empty QueueImpl throws NullPointerException where OCaml would match None.

front: Why make head and tail private in QueueImpl?
back: So only the class's methods can modify them, which lets the class guarantee its invariant.

front: Exam trap: your queue function's type says int queue.
back: Keep code generic ('a queue) unless the question fixes the type. Annotating with int can cost points.

front: Exam trap: "you may use only ...".
back: It's binding: no List.rev, @ or helpers that aren't listed. Write your own tail-recursive reverse if needed.

front: Exam trap: after removing from or truncating a queue.
back: Update tail too, set the new last node's next to None, and make head and tail both None when it becomes empty.

front: Exam time rule?
back: On a 120-point, 60-minute exam spend about 1 minute per 2 points (a 34-point problem ≈ 17 min). On a 60-point exam, 1 minute per point. Skip and return.

front: Last two minutes of the exam: what do you reread?
back: The "returns ()", "must be tail recursive", "exit early" and "may use only" lines, and every Java answer's choice of compile error vs exception vs output.
